checklist: Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. In the Content Browser, the panel that shows all your project files, find the asset named SKM_Quinn_Simple or SKM_Manny_Simple.
Drag the Skeletal Mesh from the Content Browser into the Level Viewport. Unreal creates a Skeletal Mesh Actor for you. Move it to an empty spot in the level.
With the actor selected, look at the Details panel and find the Animation section. Set Animation Mode to Use Animation Asset, which means the actor plays one animation that you choose.
Set Anim to Play to one animation from the folder Content/Characters/Mannequins/Anims. For example, you can pick an idle or a run.
Turn on Looping so the animation repeats. Then press Play and watch the mesh animate in the level.
Try one more thing: drag a different Material onto the actor. If the mesh looks wrong, open that Material and enable the option Used with Skeletal Mesh.
Create a new project from the Third Person template (choose Games, then Third Person). Press Play once and move around with the WASD keys and Space.
Open the folder Content/Characters. Find the UE5 mannequins Quinn and Manny, and note which one the template uses by default.
Open the folder Content/Characters/Mannequins/Anims. Count how many animation sets there are, and open one animation from each set.
Open the Blueprint Content/ThirdPerson/Blueprints/BP_ThirdPersonCharacter. Select the Mesh component, and change its Skeletal Mesh property to SKM_Manny_Simple.
In the Animation section, set Animation Mode to Use Animation Blueprint and set Anim Class to ABP_Manny. Click Compile, save the Blueprint, and press Play.
Open the Rigs folder and find the assets CR_Mannequin_Body and CR_Mannequin_BasicFootIK. Read on the documentation page what each one is used for.

quiz.q: Which mannequin does the UE5 Third Person template use by default?
quiz.explain: The template starts with the feminine UE5 mannequin, Quinn. Manny is the male mannequin and is also included.

quiz.q: Where are the mannequin animations stored in the template?
quiz.explain: Animations for the mannequins live in Content/Characters/Mannequins/Anims. There are two sets, one per mannequin.

quiz.q: To swap the player mesh to Manny, which Blueprint do you edit?
quiz.explain: You open BP_ThirdPersonCharacter, select the Mesh component, and change its Skeletal Mesh, Animation Mode and Anim Class.

choices: Adjusting the feet to the terrain with IK
quiz.explain: The template's Animation Blueprints use the IK Rig system. CR_Mannequin_BasicFootIK adjusts the position of the feet to match the terrain.

choices: Posing and animating the mannequin directly in the editor
quiz.explain: CR_Mannequin_Body is a Control Rig asset you can use to pose and animate the mannequin in the editor.

checklist: Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Get an FBX file of a rigged character (a character that has bones) and one animation for it. If you have none, export one from Unreal: right-click SKM_Manny_Simple, choose Asset Actions, then Export, and export one animation the same way.
Make a folder named Content/Import_Test. Click Import in the Content Browser and pick the mesh FBX file.

The import window opens. In current versions it is named Interchange Pipeline Configuration, and older versions show a window named FBX Import Options. The settings you need are in both. Leave Skeleton empty and keep Create Physics Asset turned on. Find the scale settings, Convert Scene Unit and the uniform scale (named Offset Uniform Scale in the new window and Import Uniform Scale in the old one), then click Import.
Open the new Skeletal Mesh in the editor. Check that its size matches the mannequin, and check the list of bones in the Skeleton Tree.
Now import the animation FBX file on its own. This time set Skeleton to the Skeleton you just created. Confirm that an Animation Sequence asset appears.
Import the mesh a second time into another folder, but now select the existing Skeleton in the dropdown. Notice that Unreal does not create a new Skeleton asset this time.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. In the Content Browser, find the mannequin Physics Asset next to SKM_Manny_Simple. Its name starts with PA_. Double-click it to open the Physics Asset Editor.
Look at the bodies and constraints on the mannequin. Select the shoulder body and count the bodies that are below it in the hierarchy.

Open the Simulation dropdown, which is the arrow next to the Simulate button in the toolbar. Try Simulation first. Then try No Gravity and hold Ctrl while you click bodies to poke them. Then select the shoulder and try Selected Simulation.
In the Content Browser, right-click SKM_Manny_Simple and choose Create, then Physics Asset, then Create. Accept the default settings and compare the new asset with the original one.

In BP_ThirdPersonCharacter, add a key press event. On the Mesh component, call Set Simulate Physics with the value true, and set its Collision Enabled to Physics Only or Collision Enabled. Set the collision of the Capsule to No Collision.
Press Play, press the key, and watch the character fall as a ragdoll. Take a screenshot while it is falling.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. In the Content Browser, right-click any Animation Sequence of the mannequin, for example a jump, and choose Create, then Create AnimMontage. Name the new asset AM_Attack. If you have an attack animation of your own, use that.
Open the montage. Drag two more Animation Sequences from the Asset Browser into the same Slot track, so that the three animations play one after the other.
Right-click the Montage track and create three Montage Sections named Start, Loop and End. Place one section header at the start of each animation.
In the Montage Sections panel, click Clear to remove the existing links. Then link Start to Loop, and link Loop to Loop, so that the middle part repeats.
Open Window > Anim Slot Manager. Add a Slot named FullBody, and set the Slot track of the montage to DefaultGroup.FullBody. Save the Skeleton, because Slots are stored on it.

Open the Animation Blueprint that the character uses (ABP_Unarmed in the current template, ABP_Manny or ABP_Quinn in older versions). In its AnimGraph, add a Slot node just before the Output Pose node, after the locomotion and any other nodes. Set its Slot Name to FullBody.
In BP_ThirdPersonCharacter, use a Play Montage node with the character's Mesh to play AM_Attack when a key is pressed. On a second key, call Montage Jump to Section with the Section Name set to End.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Right-click any Animation Sequence of the mannequin in which the arms move, choose Create, then Create AnimMontage, and name it AM_UpperWave. If you have a wave or attack animation of your own, use that. Open the montage, open Window > Anim Slot Manager, add a Slot named UpperBody, and set the Slot track of the montage to DefaultGroup.UpperBody.

Open the Animation Blueprint that the character uses (ABP_Unarmed in the current template, ABP_Manny or ABP_Quinn in older versions). In the AnimGraph, find the last node before the Output Pose node, drag from its output and add a New Save cached pose node. Name it LocomotionCache. A cached pose stores a result so that you can use it in more than one place.
Add a Layered blend per bone node. Add a Use cached pose LocomotionCache node and connect it to the Base Pose input.
Add a second Use cached pose LocomotionCache node and connect it to a Slot node that is set to DefaultGroup.UpperBody. Connect the Slot node to the Blend Poses 0 input.

Select the Layered blend per bone node. In its Details panel, expand Layer Setup and add one entry with Bone Name spine_01 and Blend Depth 1. Also check Mesh Space Rotation Blend. Connect the output of the node to the Output Pose node.
In BP_ThirdPersonCharacter, add a key press event. First check Montage Is Playing, and then call Montage Play with AM_UpperWave only if the montage is not already playing.
Play in the editor, walk, and press the key. The legs should keep walking while the upper body plays the montage.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. You need an Animation Sequence that moves the root bone forward, such as a roll or a vault. If you have none, make one: duplicate a jump or walk animation of the mannequin and name the copy Anim_RootMove. Open it, go to the first frame, select the root bone in the Skeleton Tree and press Key in the toolbar. Then go to the last frame, move the root bone about 200 units forward in the viewport, and press Key again.
In the viewport, open the Character menu, go to Bones, then Bone Drawing, and choose All Hierarchy so that all bones are drawn. Watch the red root bone and its red line while the animation plays.
In the Character menu, go to Animation, then Root Motion, and try the options Ignore, Loop, and Loop and Reset. Note what each option does to the preview.
In the Asset Details panel, check Enable Root Motion on the sequence. The panel writes it as one word, EnableRootMotion. Then create a montage from the sequence and name it AM_Roll.

Open the Animation Blueprint that the character uses (ABP_Unarmed in the current template, ABP_Manny or ABP_Quinn in older versions) and click Class Defaults in the toolbar. Set Root Motion Mode to Root Motion from Montages Only. Also make sure the AnimGraph has a Slot 'DefaultSlot' node before the Output Pose node, so that montages are shown.
In BP_ThirdPersonCharacter, add a key press event that plays AM_Roll with a Play Montage node and the character's Mesh. Play in the editor and press the key while the character is standing still.
Open the console with the backtick key and type show collision. You can now see the capsule, the collision shape of the character, move together with the mesh.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. In the Content Browser, click Add (+), then Animation, then IK Rig. Pick the Skeletal Mesh of the character, for example SKM_Manny_Simple, and name the new asset IK_MyCharacter.
In the Hierarchy panel, right-click the pelvis bone and set it as the pelvis (the retarget root). This tells Unreal which bone carries the movement of the whole body.

Create retarget chains for Spine, Neck, Head, Left Arm, Right Arm, Left Leg and Right Leg. For each chain, select the bones from the first to the last, right-click, choose New Retarget Chain, and check the Chain Name that Unreal fills in for you.
Select both foot bones, click Add (+) in the Hierarchy panel and choose New IK Goal. When Unreal asks for a Solver, pick Limb IK. A solver is the part that calculates how the limb bends.
Do this for each Limb IK solver: select the solver and the thigh bone, right-click, and choose Set Root Bone on Selected Solver.
In the viewport, drag one foot goal up and watch the leg bend. Then click Reset.
Look at the IK Retargeting panel and check that every chain has a name, a Start Bone and an End Bone.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Build an actor that the player can interact with, named BP_Lever or BP_Chest. Give it a trigger volume and a prompt on screen. When the player presses the interact key inside the trigger volume, the actor tells the character to interact.

Create a montage named AM_Interact from one or two Animation Sequences of the mannequin, or from your own, with at least two sections, Reach and Pull. Set it to a named Slot, FullBody or UpperBody, and make sure that this Slot exists in the AnimGraph of the character.
Play AM_Interact with the Play Montage node. Use its On Completed output to unlock the player, and use On Interrupted to cancel the interaction cleanly.
Add a Notify to the montage at the moment when the hand touches the object. When that notify fires, spawn a Niagara effect or play a sound at a socket on the hand.
Add a second notify that fires On Notify Begin in the Play Montage node. Use it to change the state of the lever or chest, for example to open or pulled.
Make it possible to interrupt the montage. A hit or a jump during the montage should stop it, and the actor should go back to its starting state.
Record a short video clip (30 seconds or less). It must show the approach, the interaction, the effect at the right frame, the change of the actor state, and one attempt that is interrupted.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Set up the crowd assets: duplicate SKM_Manny_Simple and name the copy SK_CrowdCharacter, duplicate ABP_Manny and name the copy ABP_Crowd, and make a Character Blueprint named BP_CrowdCharacter whose Mesh uses SK_CrowdCharacter with ABP_Crowd as its Anim Class. Spawn 50 or more copies of BP_CrowdCharacter, for example with a loop in the Level Blueprint that calls Spawn Actor from Class in a grid. Type stat unit in the console to show the frame times, and note the game thread time.

In ABP_Crowd, open Class Settings, find the Optimization section and enable Warn About Blueprint Usage. Move the Event Graph logic into a Thread Safe function that uses Property Access. Continue until the AnimGraph nodes show the Fast Path lightning icon.

Enable the Animation Budget Allocator plugin. In BP_CrowdCharacter, select the Mesh and set its Component Class to SkeletalMeshComponentBudgeted, turn on Auto Calculate Significance, and call Enable Animation Budget at Begin Play.
Run the game with the console command a.Budget.Debug.Enabled 1, and turn on Stat, then Advanced, then AnimationBudgetAllocator. Take a screenshot of the graph and of the numbers shown over each mesh.

Open the file Config/DefaultScalability.ini and add a value for a.Budget.BudgetMs for each quality level. Each level has its own section, so you write four sections: [ViewDistanceQuality@0], [ViewDistanceQuality@1], [ViewDistanceQuality@2] and [ViewDistanceQuality@3], each with its own a.Budget.BudgetMs line below it. Test two of the levels.
Open SK_CrowdCharacter, set Number of LODs to 4 and click Apply Changes. Add Bones to Prioritize on the face or the hands with a high Weight of Prioritization, and click Regenerate LOD.
Compare stat unit before and after your changes, and write the numbers down.
Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Enable the Control Rig Modules plugin: open Edit > Plugins, look in the Animation category, enable it and restart the editor.

Create CR_Modular_Hero: in the Add menu choose Animation, then Control Rig, then Control Rig, and choose ModularRig. Set the Preview Mesh to the mannequin, for example SKM_Manny_Simple, or to a character of your own.
Drag the Spine module onto the unresolved socket. Then add Neck, both Legs, both Feet, Shoulders and Arms. For the fingers, select all finger sockets at once and drop one Finger module on them.
Delete the modules of the left arm. Build them again by selecting the modules of the right arm and using Mirror in the Module Hierarchy.

Make one connector unresolved on purpose, for example by renaming a bone or removing a socket. Then fix it with Use Selected or with the hierarchy dropdown. Take a screenshot of the red none before the fix and another one after the fix.

Create your own module. Make a new Control Rig, choose Switch to Rig Module, and set its Name, Icon and Description. Add one Secondary connector with a Type Rule, and then add your module to CR_Modular_Hero.
Drag CR_Modular_Hero into a level. Set keys for 3 poses in Sequencer, the animation timeline tool of Unreal, and take a screenshot of each pose.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Use a character whose cape, skirt or coat has its own material section, for example your own character or a free one from Fab, Epic's asset store. If you have none, you can practice on a copy of SKM_Manny_Simple: use one of its material sections as the cloth, and later paint the Max Distance mask so that only a small area, such as the lower back, is allowed to move.

In the Skeletal Mesh Editor, click Section Selection and select the cape section. Right-click it and choose Create Cloth Asset from Selection. Name the asset CA_Cape and set the Physics Asset of the character, which is used for collision.
Right-click the section again and choose Apply Clothing Asset, then CA_Cape. Open Window > Clothing and click Activate Cloth Paint.

Create a Max Distance mask. Paint the value 0 along the shoulders, so the cloth stays fixed there. Then use the Gradient tool to go down to a large value at the hem, the bottom edge of the cape. Hold H to preview the cloth.
Add a Backstop Distance mask so that the cape cannot pass into the back of the character. Then tune these Config values: Damping, Gravity Scale and Collision Thickness. Set Wind Method to Accurate.

Play the character with a run animation and a turn for about 20 seconds, and take screenshots or record a short video clip of the cloth moving. Fix one clipping problem, a place where the cloth goes through the body, by changing a mask and not the mesh.
Read the overview page of the Panel Cloth Editor in Epic's documentation. Write 3 lines about when you would use the Dataflow-based cloth asset in place of this legacy (older) tool.
Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Create a 2D Blend Space asset named BS_Strafe for the Mannequin skeleton. To do this, click Add, then Animation, then Blend Space.
In Asset Details, name the horizontal axis Direction with a range from -180 to 180. Name the vertical axis Speed with a range from 0 to 600.
Set both Axis Functions to Locomotion. Choose Rightward Speed for the horizontal axis and Forward Speed for the vertical axis. Set Bone/Socket 1 and Bone/Socket 2 to the two foot bones.
Drag idle, walk and run animations onto the graph and watch the analysis place them. If you see red triangles, which are very thin, fix them by moving the samples.
On the Speed axis, set Smoothing Time to 0.2 and Smoothing Type to Spring Damper. Hold Ctrl and move the mouse in the graph, and watch the second crosshair follow with a delay.
Set Notify Trigger Mode to Highest Weighted Animation, so that only the strongest animation fires its notifies.

Duplicate the Animation Blueprint that the character uses (ABP_Unarmed in the current template, ABP_Manny or ABP_Quinn in older versions) and open the copy. In its AnimGraph, add BS_Strafe as a Blendspace Player node. Drive its Direction and Speed inputs from variables.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Prepare 9 aim poses: center, up, down, left, right and the 4 corners. If you have no aim poses, make simple ones: open the idle animation of the mannequin, pause it, rotate a spine bone in the Skeleton Tree so that the upper body leans in one direction, click Create Asset in the toolbar, choose Create Animation, then Current Pose, and save it with a clear name such as Aim_Up. Do this for all 9 poses, with no rotation for the center pose. Open the Animation Sequence of each pose.

In each sequence, set Additive Anim Type to Mesh Space and set Base Pose Type to Selected animation frame. Set Base Pose Animation to the center pose, which aims forward, and set Ref Frame Index to 0.
Create an Aim Offset named AO_Aim for the same skeleton. To do this, click Add, then Animation, then Aim Offset. Set Preview Base Pose to the center pose.

Set both Axis Functions to Orientation. For the horizontal axis choose Axis Yaw, and for the vertical axis choose Axis Pitch. Set Bone/Socket to the bone of the hand that holds the weapon, set Bone Facing Axis to +X and Bone Right Axis to +Y.
Drag the 9 poses into the graph and let the analysis place them. If needed, correct the axis ranges so that they go from -90 to 90.

Duplicate the Animation Blueprint that the character uses (ABP_Unarmed in the current template, ABP_Manny or ABP_Quinn in older versions) and open the copy. In its AnimGraph, add AO_Aim as a player node after the State Machine. Drive its Yaw and Pitch inputs with property access from the base aim rotation of the pawn.
Set LOD Threshold on the Aim Offset node to 2, so the node stops running on the simpler, far away versions of the mesh.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Duplicate the Animation Blueprint that the character uses (ABP_Unarmed in the current template, ABP_Manny or ABP_Quinn in older versions) and open the copy. Create an enum named E_Stance with the values Unarmed, Rifle and Pistol. Then, in the Animation Blueprint, create a variable named Stance of that type.

Add a Blend Poses by Enum node after the locomotion State Machine. Connect Stance to Active Enum Value. Add a pose input for each stance by right-clicking the node and choosing Add Blend Pin. Connect the locomotion to the first input, and any two different animations of the mannequin, as Sequence Players, to the other two.
In the Details panel, show the Blend Time pins, and set a different Blend Time for each pose: 0.1, 0.3 and 0.5.
Add a Blend Poses by bool node for IsCrouched. Place an Inertialization node after it, close to the Output Pose.
Add a Blend Multi node with three inputs, and drive it with a float variable named Alpha.
In the Anim Preview Editor, change Stance and IsCrouched. Watch how the pulsing pose links change to show which pose is active.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Open the Mannequin Skeletal Mesh, for example SKM_Manny_Simple. In the Skeleton Tree, open Options and choose Add Blend Mask. Name the mask BM_UpperBody.
Right-click the bone spine_01 and use Recursively Set Blend Scales to set it and all the bones below it to 1. Set the pelvis and the leg bones to 0.

Duplicate the Animation Blueprint that the character uses (ABP_Unarmed in the current template, ABP_Manny or ABP_Quinn in older versions) and open the copy. Add a Layered blend per bone node. Set its Blend Mode to Blend Mask and pick BM_UpperBody. Connect the locomotion as the base pose, and connect a Slot node as the blend pose, so that a montage played on that slot shows on the upper body only.
Go back to the Skeleton Tree, open Options and choose Add Time Blend Profile. Name it Profile_LegsFast. Set the pelvis and the upper body bones to 1.0 and the leg bones to 0.5.

In the State Machine of the Animation Blueprint, select a transition rule, for example the one from Idle to the walk and run state, and set its Blend Profile to Profile_LegsFast. Also set the same profile on a Blend Poses by bool node.
Play in the editor. Compare how the character stops with the profile and without it.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Duplicate the Animation Blueprint that the character uses (ABP_Unarmed in the current template, ABP_Manny or ABP_Quinn in older versions), open the copy, and set it as the Anim Class of the Mesh in BP_ThirdPersonCharacter. From the Animation Blueprint, open Window > Anim Slot Manager. Add two slots named FullBody and UpperBody. Add a group named Actions, move both slots into it, and save.
In the AnimGraph, add a Slot node after the State Machine and set its Slot Name to FullBody.
Add a second Slot node and set it to UpperBody. Connect it to a Layered blend per bone node that uses a Branch Filter on spine_01, so that only the upper body plays the slot animation.

Select the FullBody Slot node and enable Always Update Source Pose in its Details panel. With this setting on, the pose that goes into the Slot node keeps updating while a montage plays over it. With it off, that source pose is not updated during the montage. Write down in one line which behavior you need for your character.

Make two montages from any two Animation Sequences of the mannequin, both in the group Actions: AM_Reload on the slot UpperBody and AM_Emote on the slot FullBody. In BP_ThirdPersonCharacter, play each one from its own key press event. Play AM_Reload, and then play AM_Emote before the first one ends. Confirm that the reload stops.
Create a Level Sequence, add the character from the level to it, and add an Animation track with any animation. Right-click the animation section, open Properties, find Slot Name and type FullBody.
Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Enable the Animation Insights plugin in Edit > Plugins, and restart the editor.

Open the Animation Blueprint that the character uses (ABP_Unarmed in the current template, ABP_Manny or ABP_Quinn in older versions). Right-click two nodes in the AnimGraph, for example the locomotion State Machine and the last node before Output Pose, and choose Toggle Pose Watch on each. Open Window > Pose Watch Manager and give each pose watch a different color.
Open Tools > Debug > Rewind Debugger and also Tools > Debug > Rewind Debugger Details. Press Play, click Record, move around, and then pause.
Pick your character with the Dropper tool. Select the Animation Blueprint track, and drag the red playhead to move through the recording.
Double-click the Animation Blueprint in the Object Outliner. It opens linked to the recording. Watch the nodes, the variables and the state machine change while you move the playhead.
During a PIE (Play In Editor) session, type ShowDebug ANIMATION in the console and take a screenshot. Also try the command DisplayAll with the class of your Animation Blueprint and one variable.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Duplicate the Animation Blueprint that the character uses (ABP_Unarmed in the current template, ABP_Manny or ABP_Quinn in older versions), name the copy ABP_ThreadSafe, and set it as the Anim Class of the Mesh in BP_ThirdPersonCharacter. Its Event Graph already has update logic that you will replace. Open it. In the My Blueprint panel, go to Functions, open the Override dropdown, and choose Blueprint Thread Safe Update Animation.

Create a function named UpdateMovement and enable Thread Safe in its Details panel. Inside the function, add a Property Access node and bind it to this path: Try Get Pawn Owner, then Get Movement Component, then Velocity.

From the velocity, use Vector Length XY and promote the result to a variable named Speed. Make a bool variable named ShouldMove that is true when Speed >= 0.1. Also read IsFalling into a bool variable.
Call UpdateMovement from Blueprint Thread Safe Update Animation. Then delete the old Update Animation event logic from the Event Graph.

Select a Blendspace Player or Sequence Player node inside the state machine, or an Aim Offset node if your Animation Blueprint has one. In its Details panel, under Functions, bind On Update to a new function. Open the function and look at its Context and Node pins: the function runs each time this node updates, and it is the place to set values for this one node, such as the Yaw and Pitch of an Aim Offset.
Enable Warn About Blueprint Usage in Class Settings and compile. Fix every warning until the lightning icon, which means Fast Path, shows on your blend nodes.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Make an additive animation: duplicate the idle animation of the mannequin, name the copy Idle_SwayAdditive, and in its Asset Details set Additive Anim Type to Local Space, with the first frame of the same animation as the base pose. Create an Animation Blueprint named ABP_Sway for the Mannequin skeleton. In its AnimGraph, add an Input Pose node from the Misc category and rename it Source. Send it through an Apply Additive node with the additive animation. Add a float variable named SwayAlpha and make it Instance Editable.

Duplicate the Animation Blueprint that the character uses (ABP_Unarmed in the current template, ABP_Manny or ABP_Quinn in older versions) and use the copy as your main Animation Blueprint. Right-click its AnimGraph, open Linked Anim Blueprints and choose Linked Anim Graph. Set its Instance Class to ABP_Sway. Connect the locomotion to the Source pin and set SwayAlpha on the node.

Create a Template Animation Blueprint named ABPT_SinglePlay. In the creation window, choose Template and do not pick a Skeleton. Add a Sequence Player. On its Sequence property, choose Bind, then Expose As Pin, and promote the pin to a public variable.
Link ABPT_SinglePlay in your main Animation Blueprint, and set the exposed Sequence variable to an animation.
On the Linked Anim Graph node, enable Receive Notifies from Linked Instances. Test it with a Skeleton Notify placed inside ABP_Sway.
Double-click the Linked Anim Graph node to jump into the linked asset, and confirm that it opens.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one, and drag SKM_Manny_Simple or SKM_Quinn_Simple into the level as a Skeletal Mesh Actor. Create a Level Sequence named LS_ClipBlend and add the mannequin Skeletal Mesh Actor to it. On its Animation track, add a walk clip at frame 0 and a run clip, placed so that the two sections overlap by about 15 frames.
Drag the blend handle on the overlap. Right-click the blend curve and change the shape of the curve under Options. Play the sequence and watch the blend.
Expand the Animation track. Set keys on the Weight of the run section so that it goes from 0 to 1 across the overlap.
Hold Ctrl on the right edge of the walk clip and drag to change its Play Rate. Then right-click the clip and use Edit, then Auto Size, to restore its length. Split a clip in two with Ctrl+/.

Put the playhead at the start of the run clip. Right-click the run clip, choose Match With This Bone In Previous Clip, and pick a foot bone or the pelvis bone. Then enable Show Root Motion Trail on the track.
Right-click a section, open Properties, and set When Finished to Keep State. Check what is different when the sequence ends.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Open a Level Sequence in which a mannequin Skeletal Mesh Actor plays a walk animation on its Animation track. To make one, drag SKM_Manny_Simple into the level, create a Level Sequence named LS_ClipBlend, add the actor, and add a walk clip. On the character track, click Add (+) Track, then Control Rig, then FK Control Rig.

Right-click the FK Control Rig track and enable Additive. Select the head bone in the viewport and set a key at frame 0, then a key with a small head tilt at frame 20, and a key back at the first pose at frame 40. Play the sequence: the tilt is added on top of the walk.
Right-click the FK track and use Select Bones Or Curves To Animate. Hide every bone except the spine, the neck, the head and the arms.
Duplicate the character in a second sequence named LS_BakeFix. Right-click the Skeletal Mesh track and choose Edit With FK Control Rig. Enable Reduce Keys with a small Tolerance, and click Create.
Fix one bad frame on the baked FK rig, for example an elbow that jumps. Then right-click the Skeletal Mesh track and choose Bake Animation Sequence. Save the result as AS_Walk_Fixed.

Now try a layered track. Drag the Control Rig asset CR_Mannequin_Body into the level, which opens a new sequence with a Control Rig track, and set two or three keys on a control. Right-click the Control Rig track and choose Convert To Layered. Check that your keys are now applied on top of an animation clip.

Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Open a Level Sequence in which a prop has keys on its Transform track. To make one, place a cube named SM_Crate, create a Level Sequence named LS_KeyDrill, add the cube, and set three keys with the S key at different frames and positions. It must be a source Level Sequence, not a shot inside a master sequence. Select the crate actor and use Actions, then Export... Read every option in the FBX Export Options window, and then export with the default settings.
Export again with nothing selected. This time the whole sequence is exported. Compare the sizes of the two files.

Open the FBX file in any DCC or FBX viewer you have. Blender is free and works well. Set the time rate of the DCC to match the frame rate of the sequence. Move the keys of the crate, and then export the FBX with Z as the up axis.
Back in Sequencer, right-click the crate track and choose Import. Look at the options Force Front XAxis and Create Cameras in the Import FBX window, and then import. Confirm that the keys changed.
Also try the import from the Actions menu with nothing selected. Note how Unreal matches objects by their names.

For a sequence with a character, for example one where you dragged SKM_Manny_Simple into the level and gave it an animation clip, right-click the Skeletal Mesh track and use Bake Animation Sequence to make an asset named AS_Export_Test. Open it in the Animation Sequence editor.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Right-click the mannequin skeletal mesh, for example SKM_Manny_Simple, and choose Create, then Control Rig. Rename the new asset CR_Manny_FKArm.
In the Rig Hierarchy, select the bones upperarm_l, lowerarm_l and hand_l. Right-click and choose New, then Add Controls For Selected.
Select the bones of the right arm, hold Alt and use the same command again. Holding Alt opens a dialog. In it, set Output Format to Hierarchy and Suffix to _ctrl.
Create a Null named arms_grp. Drag the top control of each arm onto it, so that both become its children.
Select hand_l_ctrl. In the Details panel, set Value Type to Rotator, so that this control can only rotate.
Select upperarm_l_ctrl. Under Transform, click Min and Max, enable the Z rotation channel, and set the limits to -50 and 50. Enable Draw Limits to see them in the viewport.

In the graph, add a Set Transform node for each bone and connect a Get Transform node of its control to it. Connect all of them in a chain that starts at Forwards Solve. Move a control in the viewport to test the rig.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Open a Control Rig that has at least four controls, with some on the left and some on the right side of the body. If you have none, make one: right-click SKM_Manny_Simple, choose Create, then Control Rig, select the upper arm and hand bones of both arms in the Rig Hierarchy, right-click and choose New, then Add Controls For Selected.
Select each control in turn. In the Details panel, under Control Shape, pick a different Shape. Set the controls of the left side to blue and the controls of the right side to red.
In the Settings of the Content Browser, enable Show Engine Content and Show Plugin Content. Find the shape library in this folder: Engine, then Plugins, then Control Rig Content, then Controls.
Do not edit the library that comes with the engine. Duplicate it into your project, name the copy CRSL_Project, and open it.

Make a simple static mesh for your shape, such as a flat arrow or a ring. In Modeling Mode, the Arrow shape tool creates one for you: accept the tool and rename the new Static Mesh asset SM_CtrlArrow. You can also import an .fbx file of your own. If you do, turn off the import of materials and textures in the import window, because a control shape does not need them.

In CRSL_Project, add an element to the Shapes array (the documentation page still uses the old name, Gizmos). Set Shape Name to Arrow, set Static Mesh to SM_CtrlArrow, and set a Transform that fits the size of the mannequin.
In your Control Rig, open Class Settings and add CRSL_Project under Shape Libraries (the documentation page calls this property Gizmo Library). Then set the Shape of one control to Arrow.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Open a Control Rig that drives the arms and the head of the mannequin with FK controls. If you have none, make one: right-click SKM_Manny_Simple, choose Create, then Control Rig, and name it CR_Manny_FK. In the Rig Hierarchy, select the upper arm, lower arm and hand bones of both arms and the head bone, right-click and choose New, then Add Controls For Selected. In the graph, add a Set Transform node for each bone, connect a Get Transform node of its control to it, and connect them in a chain that starts at Forwards Solve.
Right-click the graph, open Events and add Backwards Solve. For each control, connect a Get Transform node of its bone to a Set Transform node of the control.
In the toolbar, switch Solve Direction to Backwards Solve. In Preview Scene Settings, set Preview Controller to Use Specified Animation and pick a walk animation.
Confirm that the border of the viewport is yellow and that the controls follow the animation. Then try the option Backwards and Forwards, and note the blue border.
Create a Level Sequence named LS_BakeTest. Drag SKM_Manny_Simple into the level, add this actor to the sequence, and add the same walk animation to its Animation track.
Right-click the character track, choose Bake To Control Rig, and pick your rig. Enable Reduce Keys with a Tolerance of 0.1, and click Create.
Move one baked key on an arm control to change the walk. Move the playhead through the sequence to see the change.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. In the Content Browser, click Add, then Animation, then Control Rig. Choose ControlRig and name the asset CR_FunctionLibrary. Do not assign a skeletal mesh to it.
In the My Blueprint panel, add a function named SetControlsVisible. In the Details panel, set its Access Specifier to Public so that other rigs can use it.
Select the Entry node of the function and add two inputs. The first is named Items, with the type Rig Element Key, set as an Array. The second is named Visible, with the type Boolean, set as Single.
Inside the function, add a For Each node and a Set Control Visibility node. Connect them between the Entry node and the Return node.
In Node Settings, set Category to Team, add the Keywords 'hide show', and write a Description. Also give the node a color.

Open a character rig that has hand controls. If you have none, make one: right-click SKM_Manny_Simple, choose Create, then Control Rig, select the two hand bones in the Rig Hierarchy, right-click and choose New, then Add Controls For Selected. Right-click the graph, open the Team category and choose SetControlsVisible. Connect it to Forwards Solve and give it an array of hand controls.
Right-click the shared node and choose Localize Function, which makes a local copy inside this rig. Compare the local copy with the shared version.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Create a Control Rig named CR_Manny_LookAt for the mannequin: right-click SKM_Manny_Simple and choose Create, then Control Rig. Add a Vector variable named LookTarget and a Float variable named LookWeight. Click the Eye icon next to each one in My Blueprint to make them instance-editable.
On Forwards Solve, aim the head bone at LookTarget. You can use an Aim node or your own rotation logic. Blend the result by LookWeight.
Open ABP_Manny, or make a new Animation Blueprint. In the Anim Graph, right-click, open Misc and add a Control Rig node. Place it after the locomotion pose and before the Output Pose.
In the Details panel of the node, set Control Rig Class to CR_Manny_LookAt. Under Input, enable Use Pin for LookTarget and for LookWeight.
In the Event Graph, on each update, set LookTarget to the location of the player camera and set LookWeight to 1.
Add a Float animation curve to one animation. On LookWeight, choose that curve with Use Curve and stop using the pin. Compare the result.
Disable Transfer Pose in Global Space, and check that the result is the same on this skeleton.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Open a Control Rig for the mannequin. If you have none, right-click SKM_Manny_Simple, choose Create, then Control Rig, and open the new asset. In the My Blueprint panel, add a variable named RestPose with the type Rig Pose.

Drag RestPose into the graph and choose Set. Add a Get Pose Cache node and connect its Pose pin to the Value pin. Connect the Set node to the Construction Event, so that the starting A-pose is stored. The documentation page still uses the old name of this event, Setup Event.

Add a second Rig Pose variable named ArmsPose. Fill it with a Get Pose Cache node that has Element Type set to Bones, and whose Items to Set input comes from a Get Children node of the left upperarm bone.
On Forwards Solve, add an Apply Pose Cache node that reads RestPose. Add a Float variable named RestWeight and connect it to the Weight pin.
In Preview Scene Settings, set a walk animation as the Preview Controller. Change RestWeight from 0 to 1 and watch the rig blend to the A-pose.
Add a Draw Pose Cache node for ArmsPose, and confirm that only the elements of the arm are drawn.
Add a Branch node so that RestPose is only stored when a Bool variable named StorePose is true.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Create an IK Rig named IK_Reach for the mannequin: click Add (+), then Animation, then IK Rig, and pick SKM_Manny_Simple. Select hand_r, right-click, choose New IK Goal and pick Limb IK as the solver. Then select upperarm_r, right-click and choose Set Root Bone on Selected Solver. If you already have an IK Rig with a Limb IK on the right arm, you can use that. Select the hand_r goal and enable Expose Position and Expose Rotation.

In the Animation Blueprint of the Third Person character, right-click the AnimGraph and add an IK Rig node from the Misc category. Set its Rig Definition Asset to your IK Rig. Place the node after the locomotion logic and before Output Pose.
In the Details panel of the node, under Goals, set the hand_r goal to Manual Input with the space World. Add a Vector variable named ReachTarget and connect it to the position pin of the goal.

Place a cube in the level as the target actor. In BP_ThirdPersonCharacter, get a reference to the cube, for example with an Instance Editable Actor variable or with Get Actor of Class, and pass its world location to the ReachTarget variable of the Animation Blueprint on every tick, or on a key press. Press Play and watch the hand follow the target.
Add a Float variable named ReachAlpha and connect it to the Position Alpha of the goal. Change it between 0 and 1, and confirm that the IK blends off and on.
Switch the space of the goal to Additive and give it a small offset. Compare this with World. Turn on Enable Debug Draw and set Debug Scale to 2 to see the goal in the viewport.
Try the Bone goal type: snap the hand goal to a socket bone such as ik_hand_r. Describe what this is useful for.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Open an IK Retargeter between two two-legged characters with different proportions, or make a new one. Manny and Quinn from the template work, because their bodies have different proportions: create an IK Rig for SKM_Manny_Simple and one for SKM_Quinn_Simple, use Auto Create Retarget Chains in each, and create an IK Retargeter with Manny as the source and Quinn as the target. Click Add Default Ops and write down the ops that appear.
Select FK Chains. Use Map All (Fuzzy), and then Hide Mapped Chains to see which chains are left without a match. Fix every unmapped chain by hand.

Select the LeftArm chain. Switch Rotation Mode between Interpolated and One to One while an animation in which the arms move plays. Then do the same on a finger chain. Note which mode fits each chain better.
On the Spine chain, set Translation Mode to Globally Scaled, then to Absolute, and then back to None. Note what looked broken.
Add a Pole Vector Alignment op below FK Chains. On LeftLeg, set Align Alpha to 1 and try a Static Angular Offset of 15. Watch the knee.
Add a Stretch Chains op. On the arm chains, set Match Source Length to 1, and then set Scale Chain Length to 1.1. Compare the position of the wrists.

Select Pelvis Motion and set Scale Vertical to 0.8. Then, on Root Motion, switch Root Motion Source between Copy From Source Root and Generate From Target Pelvis. Turn on Draw Chain Lines in the debug settings of FK Chains for your final screenshot.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Open an IK Retargeter between two characters, or make one: create an IK Rig for SKM_Manny_Simple and one for SKM_Quinn_Simple, use Auto Create Retarget Chains in each, create an IK Retargeter with Manny as the source and Quinn as the target, and click Add Default Ops. In the IK Rig of the target, give the LeftLeg and RightLeg chains an IK Goal, using Add Chain and Goal with Limb IK. In the retargeter, select Run IK Rig. Confirm that Enable IK is on for both leg chains, and that the goals are drawn when Draw Final Goals is on.

Under Run IK Rig, add a Floor Constraint sub-op. On both leg chains, turn Enable Floor Constraint on and set Alpha to 1. Enable Use Foot, and adjust Heel Offset and Toe Offset until the feet stop sinking into the floor in a walk animation.

Add a Stride Warp IK Goals sub-op. Set Direction Source to Goals and Forward Direction to Y, and enable it on the leg chains. Set Warp Forwards to 0.7 and then to 1.3, and watch the length of the steps.

Add a Speed Plant IK Goals sub-op. Read its settings, and write down which animation curve it needs and which Blend Method you would pick for a run. Leave the op disabled if your animations have no speed curve.
Open Override Sets and create a set named OS_LongStride. Right-click the Stride Warp op and add Warp Forwards to the set with the value 1.3. Turn the set on and off in the editor.
Open Variables and add a Float variable named StrideScale. Bind it to Warp Forwards inside OS_LongStride.

Create an Animation Blueprint for the target character. In its AnimGraph, add a Retarget Pose From Mesh node and set the retargeter on it. Add OS_LongStride to Override Set to Apply, and connect a variable to the StrideScale pin. To test it, make a Character Blueprint in which the source mesh plays an animation and the target mesh is a child component of it with this Animation Blueprint. Press Play and change the value.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. In the Content Browser, click Add (+), then Animation, then Mirror Data Table. Pick the Skeleton of the mannequin, or of your own character, and name the asset MDT_Character.

Open the table and check that Unreal filled in the left and right bones for you. Set Mirror Axis to X. Make sure that the central bones (pelvis, spine, neck and head) have the same bone in Name and in Mirrored Name. Add any rows that are missing.
Add one row with Mirror Entry Type set to Sync Marker (or Animation Notify) for a left and right pair that you use, for example FootL and FootR.

Duplicate the Animation Blueprint that the character uses (ABP_Unarmed in the current template, ABP_Manny or ABP_Quinn in older versions), name the copy ABP_Character and open it. Right-click the AnimGraph and add the Mirror node from the Mirroring category. Connect the locomotion pose to it. Create a bool variable named IsMirrored and connect it to the Mirror pin.
On the Mirror node, set Blend Time on Mirror State Change to 0.2. Add an Inertialization node after the Mirror node, because the blend time needs it.
Turn IsMirrored on and off in the preview. Check that the pose with the left foot forward becomes a pose with the right foot forward, and that the notifies still fire.
Optional: in a custom Notify State Blueprint, use Is Triggered By Mirrored Animation with a Branch node to decide whether a Print String runs.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Open the Physics Asset of the mannequin (its name starts with PA_ and it sits next to SKM_Manny_Simple), or the one of your own character. In the Skeleton Tree, open Options and enable Show Constraints. Select the constraint of the left elbow.

Use the 1, 2 and 3 keys to switch Swing1, Swing2 and Twist between Limited and Locked. Make a hinge, which means one of them is Limited and the other two are Locked. Set the limit angle to about 120 degrees. Rotate the constraint so that the green arc matches the way a real elbow bends.
Copy the constraint with Ctrl+C. Select the constraint of the right elbow and paste with Ctrl+V.
Simulate with No Gravity first to check the alignment, and then simulate normally. If the ragdoll shakes, add a small amount of Linear Damping and Angular Damping on the bodies.
Open Window > Profiles. Under Constraint Profiles, click New and name the profile CP_Stiff. Select both arm constraints and press Assign. Set Limit Stiffness and Limit Damping to stiffer values.

Create an Actor Blueprint named BP_RagdollPawn with a Skeletal Mesh Component that uses SKM_Manny_Simple. Set the collision of the component to Collision Enabled, and set it to ignore the Pawn channel. On BeginPlay, call Set Constraint Profile for All with CP_Stiff. Then call Set All Bodies Below Simulate Physics with the bone spine_01, New Simulate on and Include Self on. Place the Blueprint in a level, press Play and compare with the default profile.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Pick a character with a hanging part, such as a ponytail, a chain, a tail or a hose. If you have none, use the mannequin and treat its left arm, from upperarm_l down to hand_l, as the hanging chain. Right-click the Skeletal Mesh, choose Create, then Physics Asset, then Create, and name the asset PHYS_Secondary. Keep only the bodies of the hanging chain, and the bodies of the head, the back and the arms that it can touch.

In the Skeleton Tree, right-click the bodies of the chain and choose Collision, then Enable Collision All. Set their Physics Mode to Simulated. Set every other body to Kinematic, which means physics does not move it.

Set Mass (kg) so that the body nearest to the parent is the heaviest and each next body has half the mass. Set Linear Damping and Angular Damping to about 5.0 on the simulated bodies. Press Simulate to test.

Duplicate the Animation Blueprint that the character uses (ABP_Unarmed in the current template, ABP_Manny or ABP_Quinn in older versions), name the copy ABP_Character, and set it as the Anim Class of the Mesh in BP_ThirdPersonCharacter. In its AnimGraph, after the last pose node, add a RigidBody node, which also adds the conversion nodes to and from component space. Set Override Physics Asset to PHYS_Secondary. Keep Simulation Space set to Component Space.
Expand Sim Space Settings. Set Master Alpha to 1, Velocity Scale Z to 0.5, Max Angular Velocity to about 10, and Max Linear Acceleration to a few hundred. Run the game and spin the character.
In the Event Graph, add a custom event named OnTeleport that calls Reset Dynamics on the Anim Instance. Trigger this event after you teleport the character, so the simulation starts fresh.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Open the Physics Asset of the mannequin (its name starts with PA_ and it sits next to SKM_Manny_Simple) and go to Window > Profiles. Under Physical Animation Profiles, click New and name the profile PAP_UpperBody.
In the Skeleton Tree or in the Physics Graph, select spine_01 and every body below it. Press Assign. Check that the nodes in the graph change from shaded to filled.

With those bodies selected, set the profile to the starting values from the documentation page: Orientation Strength 1000, Angular Velocity Strength 100, Position Strength 1000, Velocity Strength 100, Max Linear Force 0 and Max Angular Force 0. Save the asset.

Create an Actor Blueprint named BP_PhysAnimPawn with a Skeletal Mesh Component that uses SKM_Manny_Simple. Set its collision preset so that collision is enabled, Object Type is Pawn, and the Pawn channel is ignored. Add a Physical Animation Component. Add a Name variable named BoneName with the value spine_01.

In the Event Graph, connect three nodes after BeginPlay. First, call Set Skeletal Mesh Component with the Physical Animation Component as target. Second, call Apply Physical Animation Profile Below with Body Name set to BoneName, Profile Name set to PAP_UpperBody, and Include Self on. Third, call Set All Bodies Below Simulate Physics with BoneName, New Simulate on and Include Self on.

Set the mesh to play a looping animation: set Animation Mode to Use Animation Asset and pick an idle. Place the Blueprint in a level and place a cube with Simulate Physics turned on next to it. Play in the editor and push the cube into the character. The upper body should follow the animation and also react to the hits.
Try Orientation Strength 100 and then 5000. Note how closely the pose still follows the animation in each case.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Create a Character Blueprint named BP_HitDummy. Set its Mesh to SKM_Manny_Simple with the Anim Class ABP_Manny, and set the collision preset of the Mesh so that collision is enabled and the Visibility channel is blocked. Place one in the level. In its Event Graph, add a custom event named HitBone with a Name input. In it, call Set All Bodies Below Simulate Physics on the Mesh with that bone, New Simulate on and Include Self on.

In BP_HitDummy, add a Timeline named TL_HitBlend with a length of 0.6 s and a float track that goes from 0 to 1 and back to 0. Play it from the start at the end of HitBone. On every update of the Timeline, send its value to Set All Bodies Below Physics Blend Weight for the same bone.
On the Finished output of the Timeline, call Set All Bodies Below Simulate Physics with New Simulate off, so that the simulation stops.

In BP_ThirdPersonCharacter, add a key press event that does a Line Trace by Channel from the camera forward, with Trace Complex turned on. Break the hit result, cast the Hit Actor to BP_HitDummy, take the Hit Bone Name, and call HitBone with it.

Open the Physics Asset of the mannequin. Select hand_l and hand_r and set their Physics Type to Kinematic. Set Physics Update Mode to Component Transform is Kinematic. Simulate with the jump loop animation, and watch the hands stay on the animation.
Play in the editor. Aim at the arm of the dummy and press the key, and then do the same on the leg. Check that the part that was hit blends into physics and back to the animation.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Open the Skeleton of the mannequin, or of your own character, in the Animation Editor. In the Skeleton Tree, right-click the root bone, choose Add Virtual Bone, and pick hand_l as the target. Do the same for hand_r.
Preview an animation and watch the two VB bones follow the hands. Save the Skeleton.
In the Options menu of the Skeleton Tree, choose Add Blend Mask. Name the mask BM_NoVirtualBones and set both virtual bones to 0.0.

Duplicate the Animation Blueprint that the character uses (ABP_Unarmed in the current template, ABP_Manny or ABP_Quinn in older versions), name the copy ABP_Character, and set it as the Anim Class of the Mesh in BP_ThirdPersonCharacter. In its AnimGraph, add two Slot nodes: one set to DefaultSlot and a second one named AdditiveSlot, which you first add in the Anim Slot Manager. Connect them to an Apply Additive node.
Put a Layered Blend per Bone node between AdditiveSlot and Apply Additive. Set its Blend Mode to Blend Mask and pick BM_NoVirtualBones.
Add a Two Bone IK node for each arm. Set IKBone to the hand, set Effector Location Space to Bone Space, and set Effector Target to the matching virtual bone. Enable Take Rotation from Effector Space.

Make an additive animation: duplicate an animation in which the upper body moves, such as the idle, and set Additive Anim Type to Local Space in its Asset Details. Create a montage from it, set its Slot track to AdditiveSlot, and play it from a key press in BP_ThirdPersonCharacter. Check that the hands stay where they are in the base pose.
Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. In the Content Browser, click Add, then Blueprint Class. Open All Classes and pick AnimNotify. Name the new class AN_Footstep.
In AN_Footstep, use the Override dropdown to add Received Notify. In it, print the name of the owner of the Skeletal Mesh Component, and play a sound at the foot socket.
Override Get Notify Name, so that the notify shows a clear label on the timeline.
Create a second Blueprint with the parent class AnimNotifyState and name it ANS_Trail. Override Received Notify Begin, Received Notify Tick and Received Notify End, and put a Print String in each.
Open a walk Animation Sequence of the mannequin. Add AN_Footstep at each moment where a foot lands, and add one ANS_Trail across the middle of the animation.
Select one AN_Footstep on the timeline. In the Details panel, set Notify Trigger Chance to 0.5 and Trigger Weight Threshold to 0.5. Play in the editor and watch the printed output.
Right-click the Notify area and open Manage Notifies. Use Find References on one Skeleton Notify to see where it is used.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Make a short Animation Sequence with 3 poses for one shoulder: arm down, arm forward and arm up. One way: duplicate the idle animation of the mannequin, open the copy, select upperarm_l in the Skeleton Tree, and press Key in the toolbar at the first frame. Then go to a frame in the middle, rotate the bone so that the arm points forward, and press Key, and do the same at the last frame with the arm up. Right-click the sequence and create a Pose Asset named PA_ShoulderFix.

Duplicate the Animation Blueprint that the character uses (ABP_Unarmed in the current template, ABP_Manny or ABP_Quinn in older versions) and open the copy. Add a Pose Driver node after the locomotion pose. Set its Pose Asset to PA_ShoulderFix.
Add upperarm_l as a Source Bone, the bone whose movement the node reads. Set Drive Source to Rotation and Drive Output to Drive Poses.
In the Tool dropdown, choose Copy All from PoseAsset to create the pose targets. Then choose Auto Scale.
Set Solver Type to Interpolative and enable Eval from Ref Pose. Compile, and rotate the arm in the preview to watch the poses blend.
Hold the Solo button on one Pose Target to preview only that pose. Double-click the button to lock it, and then unlock it again.
Switch Solver Type to Additive and compare the result. Note which solver is smoother with your 3 targets.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Make a Character Blueprint named BP_CrowdDummy whose Mesh uses SKM_Manny_Simple with the Anim Class ABP_Manny. Place 20 or more copies in a level, in rows that lead away from the Player Start. Press Play, type stat unit in the console, and write down the Game time.

Open BP_CrowdDummy and select the Mesh component. In the Details panel, find the Optimization section and turn on Enable Update Rate Optimizations. In the same panel, turn on Display Debug Update Rate Optimizations, which shows the update rate of each character on screen while the game runs.
Press Play. Stand close to the crowd, then walk far away from it, and watch how the debug display on the characters changes with distance. Take a screenshot at each distance.

On the same Mesh component, search the Details panel for Component Use Fixed Skel Bounds and turn it on. The component now skips the Physics Asset and uses fixed bounds from the Skeletal Mesh, so the bounds are not calculated again on every frame. To see the bounds, open the Show menu of the viewport, then Advanced, then Bounds, and compare with the option on and off.

Open the walk or run animation that the crowd plays and look at its Notifies track. Notifies run on the game thread after the animation work is done, so write one line that says which of them are Blueprint notifies and why the documentation advises notifies that are not Blueprint based.

Run stat unit again with all options on and compare the Game time with your first number. Read the part about Update Rate Optimizations on the documentation page linked on this quest, and note which plugin it recommends in place of URO for controlling how often Animation Blueprints are evaluated.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Open Edit > Project Settings and search for Skeletal Mesh Reduction. Make sure that the plugin property is set to SkeletalMeshReduction.

Duplicate SKM_Manny_Simple and name the copy SK_Character, or use the Skeletal Mesh of your own character. Open it. In Asset Details, under LOD Settings, set Number of LODs to 4 and click Apply Changes. Save the LODSettings asset next to the mesh.
Use the LOD menu of the viewport to look at LOD 1, LOD 2 and LOD 3. Write down the triangle count of each one.

In LOD Picker, enable Custom so that the sections of all LODs are visible. In LOD 3, add the head bone and both hand bones to Bones to Prioritize, set Weight of Prioritization to 5000, and click Regenerate LOD.
In the Reduction Settings of LOD 2, change Termination Criterion to Max Triangles and set a triangle count. Regenerate the LOD and compare.
In the LOD Info of LOD 3, add the finger bones to Bones to Remove and click Regenerate LOD. Check the icons of those bones in the Skeleton Tree.
Set LOD Hysteresis on LOD 1. Move the camera back and forth, and check for LOD popping, a sudden visible switch between two versions.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Make an Actor Blueprint named BP_SoundDoor with a cube mesh in the shape of a door, a Box Collision, and an Instance Editable boolean (true or false) variable named IsLocked. If you already have a door or lever Blueprint, you can use that instead.

On the Begin Overlap event of the Box Collision, add a Branch on IsLocked. After each output of the Branch, add a Play Sound at Location node. Pick a sound in its Sound pin, for example one from the Audio folder of the Starter Content, and connect Get Actor Location to its Location pin. You can also add an Audio Component and call Play on it.
Use one sound for when the door is locked and a different sound for when it opens. Place two copies in the level, one locked and one not, and test both in PIE.
Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Drag a Skeletal Mesh, for example SKM_Manny_Simple, into the level.
Create a Level Sequence named LS_CharacterTest. With the mesh selected, click Add Track (+) and choose Actor to Sequencer. Check that an Animation track and a Transform track were created.
On the Animation track, click Add Animation (+) and pick an idle clip. Then add a walk or run clip, and place it so that the two sections overlap by about 20 frames.
Drag the blend handle on the overlap to make the blend longer. Right-click the blend curve and try a different curve shape from Options.
Drag the right edge of the second clip outward so that the clip loops. Put the playhead in the middle of it and press Ctrl + / to split the section into two parts.
Right-click one section and open Properties. Set Play Rate to 0.5, and enable Reverse on the part you split off. Then play the sequence.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Build LS_First, a master sequence that is 15 seconds long. It needs a Shots track with at least 2 shots, and each shot has its own Cine Camera.
Put a character with at least one Animation clip in one of the shots, for example SKM_Manny_Simple with a walk animation. Blend or trim the clip so that it fits the shot.
Add a Camera Cuts track so that the master sequence cuts between the two cameras at a clear moment in the action.
Start LS_First from the Level Blueprint with a Box Trigger. Use Set Playback Position with the value 0 and then Play. Add an F key event that skips the sequence with Go to End and Stop.

Add LS_First to Movie Render Queue (Window > Cinematics > Movie Render Queue, with the Movie Render Pipeline plugin enabled). In the settings of the job, use a .png Sequence [8bit] export with Deferred Rendering and an Anti-aliasing setting with a Temporal Sample Count of 8, and render the full 15 seconds as a PNG sequence.
Write 5 lines that say what each shot shows and name one problem you fixed.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Open a sequence that has at least 2 shots. To make one, click Cinematics in the main toolbar, choose Add Level Sequence with Shots, set Number of Shots to 2, and add a camera to each shot. Place a hero mesh in the level as the main subject, for example SKM_Manny_Simple. In shot 1, drag a Spot Light from the Place Actors panel into Sequencer, so that it becomes a Spawnable. Name it L_Key_Shot01.
Set the Mobility of the light to Movable. Set the character or hero mesh (the main subject of the shot) to Movable too.
On L_Key_Shot01, open Light, then Advanced, and enable only Lighting Channel 1. On the hero mesh, enable Channel 1 in its Lighting category. Confirm that this light does not light the background.
Add keyframes on the Intensity track and the Light Color track, so that the key light changes during shot 1.

Add a Post Process Volume and enable Infinite Extent. Set Exposure Metering Mode to Manual and choose a fixed Exposure Compensation. Drag the playhead between the shots and confirm that the brightness does not drift.
Do the same for shot 2 with a second spawnable light. Play the sequence and check that each light exists only in its own shot.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Create a Level Sequence named LS_Follow. It needs a moving character or a prop that travels across the set. To make one, drag SKM_Manny_Simple into the level, add it to the sequence, give it a walk clip on its Animation track, and set two keys on its Transform track so that it moves about 10 m.

Add a Cine Camera Actor named CAM_Track. In Current Camera Settings, open Lookat Tracking Settings and enable Look at Tracking. Set Actor to Track to the character, and set a Relative Offset so that the head is framed. Enable Draw Debug Look at Tracking Position to check the point the camera aims at.
Set Look at Tracking Interp Speed to a value above 0. Compare how the camera follows with this value and with 0.
Set Focus Method to Tracking and choose the same actor. Enable Draw Debug Focus Plane and Smooth Focus Changes.

Place a Camera Rig Rail. Add spline points and curve the track. Attach CAM_Track by dragging it onto the rail in the Outliner. Add the rail to Sequencer and keyframe Current Position on Rail from 0 to 1.
Add a Camera Rig Crane with a second camera named CAM_Crane. Keyframe Crane Pitch, Crane Yaw and Crane Arm Length so that the camera rises and reveals the scene.
On the Transform track of one camera, right-click a rotation channel and choose Override with Double Perlin Noise. This adds small random movement for a light handheld feel. Set a low Amplitude.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Build a scene of 30 to 45 seconds named LS_Scene_Master. It needs at least 3 shots in a Shots track, and each shot is its own Level Sequence.

Put one animated character in the scene, for example SKM_Manny_Simple, with an Animation track that has at least 2 clips. Characters, cameras and shot lights must be Spawnables, which are actors that the sequence creates when it plays.
Use at least one following camera (Look at Tracking, a rail or a crane) and one static camera. Place your cuts on an action, not at random moments.
Light each shot with spawnable lights. Use a lighting channel for the hero in at least one shot. Lock the exposure with Manual metering.
Grade the picture. Use one base Post Process Volume for the look of the project, and at least one grade for a single shot with a different Priority.
Render with Movie Render Queue. Render a PNG sequence and EXR files, with a Temporal Sample Count of at least 4 and TAA disabled. Save the settings as a preset named MRQ_Scene.

Encode the PNG files to a video with any tool. Also cut a clip of 30 seconds or less from it that shows your best shots. Write a half-page breakdown with the shot list, what each camera does, what the grade does, and your render settings.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Open a sequence that has a character and at least 2 shots. To make one, click Cinematics in the main toolbar, choose Add Level Sequence with Shots with 2 shots, add a camera to each shot, and add SKM_Manny_Simple from the level to the master sequence. Add an Audio Track with Track (+) and drop a music Sound Wave at frame 0. The Audio folder of the Starter Content has music and sound effects that you can use.
Add a second Audio Track for a footstep sound or a door sound. Trim its edges, and drag its end past the length of the clip so that it loops.
Drag the upper corners of the music section to make a fade in and a fade out. Then make two clips overlap and adjust the crossfade handles.

Expand the sound-effect track and set Attach to the character. Right-click the section, open Properties, and set an Attenuation Settings asset, which makes the sound quieter with distance. Move the camera away and listen to how the sound gets quieter.
Use Start Frame Offset (hold Shift and drag) to slide the sound inside its section, so that it lands exactly on the frame of the footstep.
Add the sequence to Movie Render Queue as a job (Window > Cinematics > Movie Render Queue). Add the WAV Audio export and a .png Sequence export to the job, and render 5 seconds.

You need a supported phone or tablet with the Unreal VCam app for this quest. Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Enable the VirtualCamera, Live Link and Take Recorder plugins in Edit > Plugins and restart the editor. Drag a VCam Actor from the Place Actors panel into the level. Put the device on the same network as your PC, open the Pixel Streaming dropdown in the editor, read the Signaling Server URL, enter it in the app and press Connect.
Tap the Wrench icon to open Tools, then open Scale and Gain. Set Axis to Planar and Scale to 2, then lower Joystick Rotation Gain. Walk a few steps and compare the result with Scale 1.
Tap Stabilization. Try Rotation Stabilization at 0x and at 100x while you do a slow pan. Then enable Kill Roll and Local Space Flight Mode, and fly with the left joystick while you look down.

In the editor, place a Cine Camera Attach Mount and name it AM_Hero. Set its Target Actor to a character that moves. For example, drag SKM_Manny_Simple into the level and move it with two Transform keys in a Level Sequence, or use the player character in Play In Editor. In the app, tap the parenting dropdown and attach the camera to AM_Hero.
Create three bookmarks from different positions and move through them with Bookmark Navigation. Check Re-inherit Camera Settings and jump to a bookmark that has a different focal length.
Tap Take Recorder and record a take of 10 seconds. Open the Take Viewer, give the take two stars and a flag, and try the smoothing slider. Then open the Takes Browser and filter by flagged.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Get a character whose cape, skirt or scarf is a separate material section, for example your own character or a free one from Fab, Epic's asset store. If you have none, you can practice on a copy of SKM_Manny_Simple: use one of its material sections as the cloth, and paint the mask so that only a small area is allowed to move. Open the character in the Skeletal Mesh Editor.

Click Section Selection and left-click the cloth part. Right-click it and choose Create Cloth Asset from Selection. Name the asset CA_Cape and set the Physics Asset of the character. Then right-click again and use Apply Clothing Asset.

Open Window > Clothing and click Activate Cloth Paint. Paint the top of the cape with the value 0, so that it stays fixed, and the bottom with a higher value, so that it can move. Hold H to preview the result.
Try the Gradient tool. Click with LMB to set the start value, click with Ctrl + LMB to set the end value, and press Enter to paint. Compare this with the brush result.
Add a Mask, set its Target to Anim Drive Multiplier, and paint it. Note what this target does for cinematics.
Create a Level Sequence named LS_Cape with the character and a run clip. Drag the playhead through it and play it. Write down one setting you changed to make the cloth look better.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one, and create a Level Sequence named LS_Extras. Drag SKM_Manny_Simple from the Content Browser into Sequencer three times, so that you get three spawnable extras.
Give each extra a different idle or walk loop on its Animation track. Shift the sections in time so that the extras do not move in step with each other.

Place four more Skeletal Mesh Actors in the level and select them. Right-click the track of one extra, open Assign Actor and choose Add Selected. Notice the yellow chevron and the count next to the track name.
On the track that is now bound to several actors, key a Transform or a property once. Check that all the bound actors change.
Right-click a spawnable track, open Spawnable, and set Spawned Object Owner to External. Play, then stop. Write down what happens to the actor.
Place one more character in front as the hero, for example SKM_Quinn_Simple. Add a Cine Camera and film a shot of 5 seconds with the hero in front and the extras moving behind.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Pick a shot of 48 frames with a moving character and a Niagara effect. To make one, create a Level Sequence, click the Camera button in Sequencer, add SKM_Manny_Simple with a walk animation, and place a Niagara System made from one of the templates, such as a fountain, in view. Add the shot to Movie Render Queue. Add the Anti-Aliasing setting with Spatial 1 and Temporal 4, turn on Override Anti-Aliasing, and set the method to None. Render it to PNG. This is render A.
Render B: use Spatial 2 and Temporal 8 (16 samples in total) with the method TemporalAA. Add Console Variables and set r.TemporalAASamples to 16. Compare the edges with render A.
Render C: use the same settings as B, but delete the console variable. Look for sample positions that repeat, which you see as less smooth edges.

Add a Camera Cuts section that starts 24 frames before the start of the playback range. Enable Use Camera Cut for Warm Up and Render Warm Up Frames, and set Engine Warm Up Count to 24. Compare the Niagara effect on frame 1 with render A.
Add Debug Options and enable Write All Samples. Render only 2 frames with Custom Playback Range. Open the sample images that are saved next to the output.
Set Output Frame Step to 2 for a quick preview. Count the output files.
Switch the job to a Movie Render Graph. Show where the temporal count is set (the Sampling Method node) and where the spatial count and the AntiAliasing Method are set (the Deferred Renderer node).

Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template, and place a character or prop to light, for example SKM_Manny_Simple. Open Window > Light Mixer. Use its Add button to place three Spot Lights around the subject, and name them SL_Key, SL_Fill and SL_Rim. Aim them like a three-point rig.

Hover over a column header and click the three-dot Overflow Menu. Add the columns Intensity, Light Color and Attenuation Radius. Set the intensity of the fill light to about half of the key light, directly in the panel.

Select SL_Key, SL_Fill and SL_Rim with Ctrl-click. Right-click, choose Select or Add Collection, and name the collection ShotA_Rig. Click the collection tab and confirm that only the three lights show.
Solo SL_Rim with the dash icon under the Headphones column, so that only this light is on. Take a viewport frame. Then click the headphones icon to bring the other lights back.
Open Window > Env. Light Mixer and set Property Details to Normal. Tune the intensity of the sun (the Directional Light) so that your rig is still clearly visible.

In a Level Sequence, add SL_Key to Sequencer. Then select all three lights, right-click the binding, open Assign Actor and choose Add Selected. Key one dip of Intensity on this track, which now controls all three lights.
Write two lines about when you would mute lights (eye icon) and when you would solo them (headphones) while you light a shot.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Import 3 short footstep .wav files, or use 3 short Sound Waves from the Audio folder of the Starter Content. Create a Sound Cue named SC_Footsteps with Add, then Sounds, then Sound Cue.

In the Sound Cue Editor, add a Random node. Click Add input until it has 3 pins and connect one Wave Player to each pin. Enable Randomize Without Replacement, which plays all sounds once before any sound repeats.
Add a Modulator node after the Random node. Set Pitch Min to 0.9 and Pitch Max to 1.1. Keep Volume Min and Volume Max at the same value.

Create a Sound Attenuation asset named SA_Footsteps, which controls how the sound gets quieter with distance. Set Attenuation Function to Logarithmic, Shape to Sphere, Inner Radius to 200 and Falloff Distance to 1500. Add an Attenuation node before the Output node and set it to SA_Footsteps.
Press Play Cue several times. Watch the wires turn red and check that a different footstep plays each time.

Open a Level Sequence with a character, or make one: drag SKM_Manny_Simple into the level, create a Level Sequence, add the actor, and click the Camera button to add a camera. Under the character track, add SC_Footsteps to an Audio Track, so that the sound is attached to the character. Drag the playhead through the sequence and listen while the camera moves away.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Import or pick three short impact Sound Waves. The Audio folder of the Starter Content has some. Create a Sound Cue named SC_Hit. Add a Random node with the three waves as inputs. Set the Weights so that one wave is chosen twice as often as the others.
Add a Modulator node after the Random node. Set Pitch Min to 0.9, Pitch Max to 1.1, Volume Min to 0.8 and Volume Max to 1.0. Connect it to the Output node.

Add a Switch node before the Output node and set Int Parameter Name to Surface. Connect your SC_Hit chain to input 0 and a different wave for metal to input 1. In a Blueprint, play the cue with Spawn Sound at Location. Then call Set Integer Parameter with In Name Surface on the Audio Component that the node returns.
On the Output node, enable Override Concurrency and set Max Count to 3. Trigger the hit 10 times quickly, and compare what you hear with Max Count 1.

Make a MetaSound Source named MSS_Hit that plays a Wave Player when a Trigger Input named Impact fires. In a Blueprint, use Spawn Sound Attached and then Execute Trigger Parameter with In Name Impact.
Write 3 sentences that say what the Random node, the Modulator node and the Switch node each changed in how the hit sounds.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Pick an attack animation for the Third Person mannequin. If you have none, any short animation of the mannequin can stand in for a punch. Right-click it and create an Animation Montage named AM_Punch. Make sure that the montage plays through a slot that the Animation Blueprint of the character uses: its AnimGraph needs a Slot 'DefaultSlot' node before Output Pose.

In AM_Punch, add a notify track named Feel. Right-click at the moment the fist reaches the target, choose Add Notify, and then Play Niagara Particle Effect, and pick any Niagara System, for example one that you make from the Simple Sprite Burst template. Then add a Sound notify with any short sound and a Pitch Multiplier of 1.1. Set Attach Name to the hand socket or bone.
